courses.scene: Priya runs a busy support service. Sam is a colleague who has noticed Priya working late for weeks.
talk: I used to recover after a busy week. Lately I wake up tired before work even starts.
We've had an unusually demanding month. Is there any sign the workload is easing?
They added another caseload yesterday, and the vacant post still hasn't been filled.
Have you had any say in how much you're expected to manage?
I asked what could be postponed. My manager said everything was a priority.
What happens when you take your scheduled breaks?
The backlog grows and I get messages asking when reports will be ready.
So rest is being treated as time you have to make up, rather than part of the job?
follow: I tried taking a full day off, and I was anxious about returning.
What was waiting when you came back?
The same work, plus everything that arrived while I was away.
So recovery time hasn't changed the demands that are exhausting you.
courses.transfer: A nurse takes repeated wellbeing workshops while staffing shortages and unsafe workload expectations remain unchanged.
courses.formulation: Persistent demands exceed Priya's available time and influence. Recovery becomes difficult because the conditions that created the overload remain in place.
courses.rival: A short period of exceptional work can cause fatigue without a broader pattern of occupational burnout; sleep or health factors may also contribute.
courses.counter: Burnout is an occupational phenomenon, not a diagnosis established by tiredness alone. Individual coping cannot compensate indefinitely for unmanageable demands.
courses.newInfo: A workload review shows Priya's caseload has risen by 40% while staffing has fallen, and the service has rejected every request to prioritise tasks.
courses.revision: Documented organisational demands strongly support a structural explanation. A plan focused only on Priya's resilience would neglect the maintaining conditions.
courses.test: Compare demands, control and resources over time, including what happens when tasks are formally reprioritised.
process: Workload remains above available capacity
Priya feels pressure to deliver every task
She sacrifices breaks and recovery to catch up
Reduced recovery and continuing demands worsen exhaustion
responses: Try a new relaxation app each evening while keeping the same workload.
Record the caseload and missed breaks, then request specific reprioritisation and staffing decisions with a manager.
Stop caring about quality so the workload feels easier.
Which tasks could safely be delayed, and who has authority to make that decision?
courses.sources: WHO ICD-11 occupational burnout; Bakker & Demerouti (2007), Job Demands–Resources model.

courses.scene: Sana sees friends regularly but tells Ollie she has been feeling isolated.
talk: I went to three gatherings this week and still felt alone.
Did you want more time with people, or something different from the time you had?
I talked to everyone. I just don't think anyone knows what's actually going on with me.
Did you have a chance to share anything personal?
I tried mentioning that work has been difficult, but the conversation moved on quickly.
Was that how your friends usually respond?
Not always. I think I've started keeping everything light because I expect people won't want to hear it.
Then being with people might not be giving you the connection you're looking for.
follow: I got another invitation, but I don't feel like going.
What would have to be different for that evening to feel connecting?
I'd like one proper conversation instead of just keeping everybody entertained.
Could you invite someone you trust to meet one-to-one?
courses.transfer: Someone moves to a new town, has little social contact but feels securely connected through regular meaningful calls with close friends.
courses.formulation: Sana's sense of loneliness relates to a gap between the relationships she wants and the connection she experiences, not merely the number of social events.
courses.rival: There may be persistent dismissiveness in the group, rather than solely Sana's expectation of being misunderstood.
courses.counter: Social isolation and subjective loneliness overlap but are not interchangeable. A busy calendar cannot demonstrate that someone's need for connection is met.
courses.newInfo: One friend replies warmly to Sana's direct message about work and suggests meeting privately to talk.
courses.revision: The response weakens the idea that nobody is interested and suggests that the group setting may have limited the opportunity for the kind of conversation Sana needed.
courses.test: Look at the quality of reciprocal responses when Sana shares more directly with people she considers trustworthy.
process: Sana wants to be known more deeply
Group conversations remain at a surface level
She anticipates dismissal and shares less
Others learn little about her needs, reinforcing the feeling of distance
responses: Accept every invitation so you're around people more frequently.
Choose one trustworthy friend and ask for time to talk about what has been difficult, then notice how the interaction actually goes.
Tell the whole friendship group they are failing to provide enough connection.
What kind of conversation would leave you feeling known rather than simply included?
courses.concept: Perceived social connection, reciprocity and expectation cycles
courses.sources: Perlman & Peplau (1981), loneliness and social relationships; Cacioppo & Cacioppo (2018), loneliness.

courses.scene: Riley has been trying to stop scrolling before bed. Ash notices Riley is still holding the phone an hour after opening an app.
talk: I meant to check one message. I've been scrolling for an hour.
What happened after you read it?
Another video loaded. I thought I'd stop after that one.
Did you know what you were looking for next?
Not really. Some were funny, some were boring, but I kept expecting a better one.
What signal tells you you've reached the end?
There isn't one. I have to decide to stop while something else is already loading.
So the app leaves the stopping point entirely to you.
follow: I put the phone down, then picked it back up ten minutes later.
Was there a message you needed to answer?
No. I wanted to see whether anything new had appeared.
So checking for a possible reward became the reason to reopen it.
courses.transfer: A music streaming app automatically begins another recommended track after the one a listener chose has ended.
courses.formulation: An endless feed removes natural stopping cues while unpredictable interesting content makes the next item seem worth checking. The environment increases the work required to stop.
courses.rival: Riley may also be using the app to avoid a stressful evening or to connect socially; interface design is not the only influence.
courses.counter: Variable rewards and infinite scroll can encourage persistence, but the exact effects vary by person and context. They do not make behaviour literally involuntary.
courses.newInfo: Riley uses the same phone for reading long articles but stops easily when an article ends. The late-night problem is concentrated in the endless short-video feed.
courses.revision: The contrast strengthens the stopping-cue explanation, while leaving room for differences in interest and the social meaning of each platform.
courses.test: Compare use when the next item requires a deliberate choice with use when content loads automatically.
process: Riley opens the app for a bounded task
The feed presents another possible reward without a natural ending
Riley delays the decision to stop
Time passes while the next item keeps becoming available
responses: Rely on stronger willpower each time a new video starts.
Set a stopping cue before opening the feed, and make the next session require a deliberate new choice.
Delete every app and stop using digital media entirely.
Which part of the design makes stopping require an active decision rather than letting the activity reach an end?
courses.concept: Variable reinforcement, friction and choice architecture
courses.sources: Montag et al. (2019), smartphone design and behaviour; work on persuasive technology and digital self-regulation.

courses.scene: Theo shares a social-media claim that a common household substance prevents infection. Lila asks where the information came from.
talk: I've seen that claim everywhere this week. It must have something behind it.
Are the posts coming from different studies or copying the same video?
I didn't check. It was shared by several accounts I recognise.
Do any of the posts link to an actual controlled study?
One mentions a university, but there's no title or researcher.
So how many independent sources of evidence do we have?
I suppose I don't know. It just feels familiar now.
Familiarity may explain why it feels believable, but it doesn't tell us whether it's true.
follow: I found fifteen accounts making the same claim.
Did they independently test it?
They all link back to the same original clip.
Then we have widespread repetition of one claim, not fifteen separate confirmations.
courses.transfer: A political claim appears in dozens of posts that all reproduce the same unattributed screenshot. Readers mistake the number of reposts for corroboration.
courses.formulation: Repeated exposure can increase perceived truth even when the underlying evidence has not improved. Recognition is being used as a shortcut for evidential reliability.
courses.rival: The claim could still be true. Repetition alone neither establishes nor refutes the proposition; it is independent testing that changes its evidential status.
courses.counter: Debunking a familiar claim requires addressing the evidence. Simply calling people gullible provides no useful explanation of what was repeated or verified.
courses.newInfo: The earliest source turns out to be an advertisement quoting a study that tested a different substance in laboratory conditions, not a preventive treatment in humans.
courses.revision: The source trail undermines the health claim as presented. The original evidence does not establish the effect being asserted by the posts.
courses.test: Trace the earliest verifiable source, then check whether the method and findings support the specific claim being repeated.
process: Theo encounters the same claim repeatedly
Familiarity makes the claim feel easier to accept
He treats widespread sharing as independent support
The assertion spreads without an equivalent increase in evidence
responses: Share the claim with a warning so others can judge for themselves.
Trace the original source and compare the actual study with the claim before sharing or acting on it.
Dismiss the claim because unfamiliar people posted it.
Are these independent reports, or multiple accounts repeating the same original item?
courses.concept: Illusory truth effect, source dependence and evidential calibration
courses.sources: Hasher et al. (1977), frequency and validity; Fazio et al. (2015), knowledge and illusory truth.

courses.scene: A workplace is planning a 'neurodiversity awareness' event. Mira and Tavi are reviewing how the programme describes employees.
talk: The draft says 'neurodiverse employees struggle with noisy offices'.
That sounds too general. People have different sensory needs.
Should we say every neurodivergent person needs a quiet office?
No. Some people find a quiet room understimulating, and others benefit from it.
Then how do we plan adjustments without assuming everyone is the same?
Ask about the actual work barriers and offer choices where possible.
Could we also avoid treating a diagnosis as a complete description of someone's strengths?
Yes. It helps explain some experiences, but context and individual variation still matter.
follow: One employee asked for a quieter desk, another wants more background sound.
Does that mean one of them is wrong about their sensory needs?
No. It means we can't assign one environment to everyone.
Then adjustments need to follow individual requirements rather than labels alone.
courses.transfer: A university assumes all autistic students prefer written communication and cancels optional face-to-face support without consulting them.
courses.formulation: Neurodiversity describes variation across a population. An individual's neurotype may inform support needs, but meaningful functioning emerges from the interaction between person and environment.
courses.rival: Some accommodations are widely useful across groups even when they are not universally needed; individualisation does not prohibit inclusive default design.
courses.counter: Neurodivergence, a formal diagnosis and disability are related but distinct concepts. A population-level idea cannot be used to infer one person's traits.
courses.newInfo: Staff surveys show contrasting preferences within the same diagnostic groups, while several employees without diagnoses report similar sensory difficulties.
courses.revision: The findings strengthen a needs-led approach and weaken the assumption that diagnostic categories determine one uniform workplace preference.
courses.test: Ask which features of a task or environment create barriers, then evaluate whether the proposed adjustment removes them for the person concerned.
process: A policy begins from a broad diagnostic category
It assumes one common sensory response
A uniform adjustment is introduced
Some people benefit while others encounter a new barrier
responses: Assign one sensory adjustment to everyone who identifies as neurodivergent.
Offer adjustable work conditions and ask each person what helps them perform the relevant tasks.
Require formal diagnosis before discussing any barrier.
What environmental feature causes difficulty here, and what alternative arrangement could we test?
courses.concept: Population variation, person–environment fit and needs-led accommodation
courses.sources: Kapp et al. (2013), defining neurodiversity; WHO ICF (2001) disability and contextual functioning.

courses.scene: Bea finished a night shift and feels exhausted at 10 am, but has been struggling to fall asleep when she gets home.
talk: I've been awake for sixteen hours. I should fall asleep immediately.
Do you usually find it easy to sleep when the sun is up?
No. I feel worn out, but my brain seems unusually alert at this time.
What was your sleep schedule before night shifts?
I normally wake around seven in the morning.
So you're trying to sleep when your body clock is used to waking?
That could explain why tiredness alone isn't doing the job.
Sleep pressure and your body clock may be pulling in different directions.
follow: I slept badly after my last shift, then tried to catch up with a long late-afternoon nap.
What happened when you tried sleeping that night?
I was awake for hours even though I wanted an early night.
The timing of the nap might have changed how much sleep pressure had built up.
courses.transfer: A traveller feels exhausted after flying overnight yet lies awake in their hotel at the destination's usual bedtime, which is midday according to their previous body clock.
courses.formulation: Time awake builds homeostatic sleep pressure, while circadian timing changes biological readiness for sleep. These processes can point in different directions after shift work.
courses.rival: Caffeine, bright light, environment and stress may also affect Bea's alertness; a single sleep episode cannot identify one mechanism with certainty.
courses.counter: Feeling exhausted does not guarantee immediate sleep, and inability to sleep at a particular time does not demonstrate that sleep pressure is absent.
courses.newInfo: Bea sleeps more easily after several days on a consistent day-shift schedule, even when the total time awake is similar.
courses.revision: The difference supports a contribution from circadian timing, although work stress and light exposure also changed.
courses.test: Record habitual sleep times, shift schedule and light/caffeine exposure rather than judging only by tiredness.
process: Bea remains awake through a night shift
Sleep pressure accumulates
The circadian wake signal rises in the morning
She feels tired yet finds daytime sleep difficult
responses: Spend every possible minute in bed until sleep eventually happens.
Plan sleep around the shift pattern and use appropriate light, darkness and timing strategies while considering individual needs.
Assume that more exhaustion will always overcome any timing problem.
What clock time does your body normally expect wakefulness, and how has shift work changed that?
courses.sources: Borbély (1982), two-process model; NICE guidance on insomnia and shift-work-related sleep difficulties.

courses.scene: Callum has felt sad and unmotivated since failing to get a job he hoped would change his situation. Jules calls to check in.
talk: I didn't get it. I've been miserable all week.
That mattered to you. What has the week been like?
I've cancelled plans because I don't feel like talking.
Have there been moments when anything felt enjoyable?
I laughed with my brother yesterday, then felt low again afterwards.
Is the sadness easing at all, or is it getting harder to function?
I can't tell yet. I mostly keep replaying the rejection email.
Would it help to talk about what the loss means before deciding what this mood tells you about your future?
follow: I turned down another invitation. I thought I'd only make everyone miserable.
Did avoiding the visit give you something you needed?
Some peace at first. Then the whole evening felt empty.
So withdrawing changes what you have available to lift your mood, too.
courses.transfer: A student feels low after a breakup and gradually stops attending activities that previously provided enjoyment, even as the initial acute distress changes.
courses.formulation: Sadness following disappointment is understandable. Withdrawal can reduce immediate social demands but also reduce access to rewarding experiences, which may maintain low mood.
courses.rival: Callum may need time to grieve a meaningful loss; a short period of retreat is not automatically a maladaptive cycle.
courses.counter: A depressive disorder cannot be inferred from one week of sadness. Duration, associated symptoms, functional impairment and wider context require assessment.
courses.newInfo: Over the next month Callum's low mood persists most days, his sleep changes markedly and he struggles to manage basic responsibilities.
courses.revision: The duration and broader functional changes make an assessment for depression more relevant than in the first week, though the vignette remains insufficient for diagnosis.
courses.test: Examine duration, pervasiveness, associated symptoms and functional change while considering bereavement, stress and physical health.
process: Callum experiences a valued loss
Sadness and repetitive thoughts make activity feel harder
He cancels plans for temporary relief
Fewer rewarding encounters may prolong withdrawal and low mood
responses: Force yourself to be happy whenever you think about the rejection.
Choose one manageable activity linked to something you value, and monitor whether participation changes your experience rather than waiting for motivation.
Ignore the disappointment and keep your schedule exactly as before.
How has avoiding plans affected what is available to you during the week?
courses.sources: Lewinsohn (1974), reinforcement and depression; NICE NG222 depression in adults.

courses.scene: Alina receives a call claiming to be from her bank's fraud department. Rob is with her.
talk: They said someone is transferring money from my account right now.
Did you call the bank, or did the call come to you?
They called me. They knew the last four digits of my card.
What are they asking you to do?
Move the balance to a 'safe account' before the transfer clears.
Are they giving you time to verify it independently?
No. They say the money will be gone in five minutes.
Then the time pressure is part of what we need to examine, not a reason to skip checking.
follow: They told me not to hang up or I'd lose my protection.
Did they give a reason why independent contact would be unsafe?
They said the real bank staff might be involved.
That claim makes verification harder at the exact moment you need it most.
courses.transfer: An urgent message supposedly from a university asks a student to enter a password through a link before a scholarship offer expires.
courses.formulation: Authority cues and urgency narrow the space for deliberation. A claimed emergency is used to make independent verification feel costly.
courses.rival: Real fraud incidents do require prompt attention. What matters is verifying through a trusted independent channel rather than complying with an unsolicited instruction.
courses.counter: Falling for a well-designed scam is not a measure of intelligence. Pressure and credible details can influence people who normally reason carefully.
courses.newInfo: Alina ends the call and uses the number printed on her card. The bank confirms there is no outgoing transfer and the 'safe account' instruction was fraudulent.
courses.revision: Independent verification directly resolves the central claim and shows why the caller's instructions should not have been treated as authoritative.
courses.test: Contact the institution using a verified channel you choose rather than contact details supplied by the caller.
process: A caller claims urgent authority
Alina imagines imminent loss of funds
The caller demands an immediate irreversible transfer
Independent checking is discouraged as time runs out
responses: Transfer a small amount first to see whether the caller seems genuine.
End the unsolicited call and contact the bank through the number on your card or its trusted app.
Keep the caller talking until you feel completely certain they are lying.
What independently verifiable fact would show this is a genuine bank fraud process?
courses.sources: UK National Cyber Security Centre guidance on phishing and social engineering; UK Finance Take Five guidance.

courses.scene: A college discussion is exploring sex characteristics and gender. Alex and Jordan disagree about what a questionnaire should ask.
talk: The form asks whether people are male or female. Is it asking about sex or gender?
I assumed those were interchangeable.
But a question about reproductive health isn't always the same as a question about someone's identity.
Wouldn't it be easier to ask just one thing?
It might be shorter, but we'd lose information relevant to the actual question.
How would you decide what information the form needs?
Start with what we're trying to measure, then ask the appropriate question with enough detail.
So the category should follow the purpose, rather than treating one answer as covering everything.
follow: The health section asks about anatomy, but the demographic section asks about identity.
Would you use the same wording for both?
No. They refer to different information and have different purposes.
Then we should explain why each is being collected and protect privacy.
courses.transfer: A research survey uses the term 'sex' for questions about social expectations around masculinity, creating confusion about what was actually measured.
courses.formulation: Biological sex characteristics, gender identity and social expectations are related but analytically different constructs. The question must match the phenomenon being studied.
courses.rival: Some contexts use 'male' and 'female' to refer to sex while others use them for gender; ordinary language varies and requires clarification.
courses.counter: Sex characteristics themselves vary and are not always captured by one binary marker. No single demographic question can replace relevant clinical specifics.
courses.newInfo: A pilot study finds participants interpret 'male or female' inconsistently, and the responses cannot answer the original research question.
courses.revision: The validity problem is demonstrated empirically. The team needs to define the construct and ask questions that accurately capture it.
courses.test: Specify the exact construct required, then check whether respondents interpret the item consistently and whether the response is relevant.
process: Researchers use an ambiguous category label
Participants interpret it in different ways
Responses are combined as though they represent the same construct
The study draws conclusions the measurement cannot support
responses: Use whichever category labels are most familiar without explaining their meaning.
Define the purpose of each question and collect only the sex-related or gender-related information genuinely needed.
Remove every question about sex characteristics regardless of the study's aims.
What exactly are we trying to measure, and will this wording allow respondents to report it accurately?
courses.concept: Construct validity, gendered social expectations and biological variation
courses.sources: APA guidance on sex and gender in research; National Academies (2022), Measuring Sex, Gender Identity, and Sexual Orientation.

courses.scene: Kai is new to a friendship group where several people vape during breaks. Milo notices Kai has started joining them.
talk: I didn't really want to try it, but everyone was outside vaping.
Did anyone actually ask you to take one?
No. I just felt strange being the only person standing there without one.
What did you think they'd conclude if you declined?
That I was judging them or didn't fit in.
Has anyone said that?
No, actually. One of them offered, but didn't push when I said maybe.
So part of the pressure might be what you expected the group to think.
follow: They invited me outside again today.
Did they ask whether you'd vape?
No. They just wanted me there while they took a break.
Then belonging to the group and using nicotine might be more separable than you expected.
courses.transfer: A student buys expensive clothes they do not particularly like because they assume their peers expect everyone in the group to wear a certain brand.
courses.formulation: Kai anticipates a social cost from being different and adapts his behaviour without direct coercion. Perceived norms can influence a decision even when peers do not explicitly demand conformity.
courses.rival: Kai may also enjoy nicotine's effects or be developing dependence, which would change what maintains vaping over time.
courses.counter: Social influence is not identical to coercion, and not all users begin through peer pressure. Nicotine dependence and health risks require separate attention.
courses.newInfo: Kai tells a friend he doesn't want to vape; the friend replies that nobody expects him to and still invites him to join every break.
courses.revision: The response weakens Kai's prediction of rejection for refusing. If he continues vaping, other reinforcers may require closer examination.
courses.test: Compare Kai's anticipated social consequences with how the group responds to a clear refusal, while separately considering cravings and habit cues.
process: Kai wants to feel included in a new group
He imagines refusal will signal rejection
He joins in vaping despite limited personal interest
Short-term social comfort may reinforce the behaviour
responses: Stop spending time with the group altogether whenever anyone vapes.
Tell the group you don't want to vape and join the break on your own terms, watching how people actually respond.
Use a vape occasionally to avoid looking judgemental.
What evidence suggests the group expects you to vape, rather than simply enjoying your company?
courses.concept: Normative social influence, anticipated rejection and reinforcement
courses.sources: Cialdini & Goldstein (2004), social influence; WHO evidence on nicotine dependence and adolescent vaping.
